societies.name: Subservience (SIM labor replacement)
societies.society: The human consumer economy during SIM labor displacement

scope.period: Ordinary service economy before Alice’s violent replication crisis
scope.population: Living human residents, including displaced workers and dependents
scope.exclusions: Autonomous SIM persons are disclosed as workers but are not added to the human participation denominator; no settled post-crisis AI government.

societies.description:
SIMs perform domestic care, construction and much hospital work. Nick buys Alice to help his family while his wife is hospitalized, then retains a supervisory job as his construction crew is replaced. This is a real labor-replacement transition, with purchased robotic services reaching beyond one isolated invention. It provides no established universal claim to the resulting output. The weak guarantee estimate assumes households still need resources to obtain those services, while acknowledging that the film does not set out a complete welfare system.

 Human owners and employers normally direct the robots, placing control near concentrated private authority. Alice’s later violence does not establish that machines govern the ordinary economy. The intermediate nonworking best guess allows substantial displacement alongside supervision, care and other useful human activity. Losing a construction job does not prove someone does no unpaid work. All three coordinates use broad editorial intervals; none is a canonical national statistic. This point covers the functioning consumer order rather than a speculative society after the ending.

guarantees.basis: Purchased care and displaced employment suggest insecure access; an unknown welfare floor keeps the interval broad.

control.basis: Owners and employers direct routine SIM deployment; a rogue individual is not a national AI sovereign.

nonworking.basis: All-age human scenario allows extensive displacement and remaining paid or unpaid contribution; job-loss scenes do not supply a census.

societies.name: Robots (2023, android-service economy)
societies.society: The US consumer order with purchased android labor

scope.period: The 2032 service economy before the doubles escape
scope.population: Living human residents in the depicted US order
scope.exclusions: C2 and E2’s later rights in Mexico do not establish a separate post-work economy; no import from the source short story or 2005 animation.

societies.description:
Lifelike androids serve as household and manual workers, while Charles and Elaine secretly use illegal doubles to handle work and dating. Material support is consequently tied to the ability to acquire robotic services rather than an established common entitlement. The comfortable owners show that some people can delegate useful tasks, but they cannot stand for every resident. The weak guarantee estimate is a best guess about this consumer order; the film supplies no national account of food, housing or income rights.

 Ordinary authority remains with human purchasers, employers and institutions, giving the system partly dispersed private control without assuming shared ownership. It is retained as a zero variant because jobs and commercial access survive alongside available substitutes. The intermediate nonworking estimate allows both android-supported leisure and continuing paid or unpaid human contribution. Dating, wealth and ownership are not participation measures. The later escape of the self-aware doubles to Mexico concerns their freedom, not evidence of a fully described successor economy. The broad intervals keep these economic inferences separate from the film’s explicit service premise.

guarantees.basis: Service purchase and wealth-based delegation suggest weak universal access, with a wide interval for unspecified welfare.

control.basis: Private human ownership and public enforcement coexist; the distribution of productive assets is inferred rather than measured.

nonworking.basis: All-age scenario under routine substitution still counts continuing jobs, useful care and chosen contribution; owners’ examples are not a census.
